title: First Sentences
subtitle: Ten sentences from Familia Romana. Read aloud first, parse never.
objectives: Read aloud ten connected Latin sentences with correct pronunciation and stress.
Understand the meaning of each sentence from context and glosses.
Recognize the subject-verb-object structure without formal parsing.
Build confidence in reading Latin for meaning before grammar.

sections.heading: Reading before parsing
sections.body:
From this lesson forward, you will read Latin for meaning. Do not parse. Do not translate word-by-word into English. Do not ask yourself what case or tense a word is in. Just read, and let the meaning emerge.

This is the natural method. Children do not learn their native language by parsing; they learn by hearing and reading connected text until patterns become intuitive. You will do the same. Grammar comes later, to name what you already recognize.

The ten sentences below come from the first chapter of Hans Ørberg's Lingua Latina per se Illustrata: Familia Romana. They are simple, repetitive, and cumulative. Each sentence adds one new word or structure. By the tenth sentence you will have read the same words five or six times, and they will begin to stick.

sections.heading: The ten sentences
sections.body:
Rōma in Italiā est.
Italia in Eurōpā est.
Graecia in Eurōpā est.
Italia et Graecia in Eurōpā sunt.
Hispānia quoque in Eurōpā est.
Hispānia et Italia et Graecia in Eurōpā sunt.
Italia paeninsula est.
Etiam Graecia et Hispānia paeninsulae sunt.
Arabia et Aegyptus in Āfricā sunt.
Āfrica nōn in Eurōpā est.

Gloss:
  Rōma — Rome (a city)
  Italia — Italy
  Eurōpa — Europe
  Graecia — Greece
  Hispānia — Spain
  Āfrica — Africa
  Arabia — Arabia
  Aegyptus — Egypt
  est — is
  sunt — are
  in — in
  et — and
  quoque — also
  nōn — not
  paeninsula — peninsula
  paeninsulae — peninsulas
  etiam — also, even

sections.heading: Listening drill
sections.instructions: Each sentence is read twice: once slowly, once at normal speed. Follow along with the text. Then read each sentence aloud yourself.

sections.heading: What you have learned without parsing
sections.body:
You have now read ten sentences of Latin. You did not parse a single word. You did not memorize a single paradigm. Yet you understand:
  — 'est' means 'is' and 'sunt' means 'are'.
  — 'in' means 'in' and 'et' means 'and'.
  — Proper nouns (Rome, Italy, Greece) are recognizable without translation.
  — Word order is flexible: 'Rōma in Italiā est' and 'in Italiā Rōma est' would both be correct.
  — The verb often comes last.

You also know, without being told, that 'paeninsula' is singular and 'paeninsulae' is plural, because 'est' pairs with the first and 'sunt' with the second. This is pattern recognition. It is how children learn language. It is faster and more durable than memorizing tables.

sections.heading: Self-check
sections.instructions: Without looking back, answer each question in English.

items.prompt: What kind of landform is Italy?
Are Spain and Greece also in Europe?

sections.heading: Read aloud again
sections.instructions: Now that you have checked your understanding, read all ten sentences aloud one more time. Aim for fluency. Do not pause between words. Let the rhythm emerge.

words.latin: Italia et Graecia in Eurōpā sunt.
words.gloss: Italy and Greece are in Europe.

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Stage 1 is complete. You can now read Latin aloud with correct pronunciation, stress, and rhythm. Stage 2 begins the grammar: the first declension, the four conjugations, and the structure of the Latin sentence.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark the lesson complete when you can read all ten sentences aloud without hesitation and understand their meaning without translating.
